about: Hook formulas for the first three seconds of a video (LIBRARY-PLAN.md phase 1). Each is a pattern to write from in the brand's own words, never a line to copy. Every formula is "untested": the library says what a formula is, never that it works; what worked for a brand is in that brand's ledger. Use: node tools/hooks/hooks.mjs find. Credits: CREDITS.md.

families.name: Question
families.what: asks what the viewer already wants answered

families.name: Contrarian
families.what: says the opposite of what the viewer believes, and means it

families.name: Outcome first
families.what: shows or states the result before anything else

families.name: Problem
families.what: names a pain the viewer recognises as theirs

families.name: Curiosity gap
families.what: opens a gap with a shape: the kind of answer is named, the answer is not

families.name: Proof
families.what: leads with a number, a result or a receipt that can be shown

families.name: Story
families.what: starts in the middle of something that happened

families.name: How to
families.what: promises a method the viewer can use

families.name: Mistake or warning
families.what: points at a mistake or a loss the viewer may be making

families.name: Callout
families.what: names the exact people it is for

families.name: Comparison
families.what: sets two things side by side: before and after, this or that

families.name: Offer
families.what: is the deal itself, said plainly

families.name: Demonstration
families.what: shows the product doing the thing, before any talk

families.name: Pattern interrupt
families.what: opens on a picture or a move the feed does not usually show

sources.name: Written for this studio
sources.copyright: Copyright 2026 the owners of this repository

formulas.name: Audience, then reason
formulas.spoken: {Audience}: the reason {shared problem} isn't what you think.
formulas.example: New managers: the reason your team goes quiet in meetings isn't what you think.
formulas.first_frame: The audience label as the first text, with the problem scene behind it.
formulas.trap: Naming a broad audience loses the point; narrow the audience label.

formulas.name: If this, watch
formulas.spoken: If you {specific situation}, this {short time} fixes it
formulas.example: If you get plenty of sign-ups but nobody finishes setup, this two-minute change fixes it
formulas.first_frame: The viewer's exact situation shown as a screen, such as a drop-off chart
formulas.trap: A situation so broad it qualifies nobody. 'If you want to grow' is not a situation.

formulas.name: If you, then the cause
formulas.spoken: If you {specific situation}, {thing} is the problem.
formulas.example: If your team keeps asking where the latest file is, your folder naming is the problem.
formulas.first_frame: A screen showing exactly that situation, such as a cluttered shared folder.
formulas.trap: A callout so broad it fits anyone fits no one; narrow it.

formulas.name: Say the feeling
formulas.spoken: If {private feeling in the audience's own words}, this is for you.
formulas.example: If opening the shared inbox makes your stomach drop, this is for you.
formulas.first_frame: The thing causing the feeling on screen, such as an overflowing inbox.
formulas.trap: Use their real words from reviews and comments, not a paraphrase.

formulas.name: Role callout
formulas.spoken: Attention {role}: {specific situation}.
formulas.example: Attention team leads: you're still copying the same update into three places.
formulas.on_screen: Team leads, one update, three places
formulas.first_frame: A screen of the exact duplicated task the role does.
formulas.trap: Reads like an ad on cold audiences; make the situation more specific than the role.

formulas.name: If you, stop scrolling
formulas.spoken: If you {audience-defining behaviour}, stop scrolling.
formulas.example: If you run payroll for a team under twenty, stop scrolling.
formulas.first_frame: The specific audience situation on screen, with motion in frame one.
formulas.trap: The source treats imperative openers as high-variance: only use it when the payoff earns the command.

formulas.name: The callout
formulas.spoken: {Specific group}, this is the one you have been ignoring
formulas.example: Support leads, this is the report you have been ignoring
formulas.on_screen: Support leads, this one is for you
formulas.first_frame: The group named in large type, with a screen they would use behind it
formulas.trap: A group so large it is not a callout. 'Entrepreneurs' is not a group.

formulas.name: This is for
formulas.spoken: This is for the {type of person} who {relatable struggle}
formulas.example: This is for the founder who keeps re-explaining the same feature on every call
formulas.first_frame: The person's exact moment shown on screen, such as a repeated call
formulas.trap: A struggle so general it fits everyone. Pick one moment they would recognise.

formulas.name: Head to head
formulas.spoken: {A} versus {B}. I ran both for {time} and one of them was not close
formulas.example: Email onboarding or in-app tips? I ran both for a month
formulas.first_frame: Both options side by side in a split screen
formulas.trap: Refusing to pick. A comparison with a diplomatic ending is a video with no ending.

formulas.name: Two states, one beat
formulas.spoken: {Before state} on one side, {after state} on the other.
formulas.example: Our old inbox on one side, the sorted one on the other.
formulas.first_frame: Both states in the frame at once, side by side or split.
formulas.trap: The change must be shown honestly; an exaggerated after is a compliance and trust problem.

formulas.name: Most do this, some do that
formulas.spoken: Most {roles} do {X}. The ones who {result} do {Y}.
formulas.example: Most project leads give status updates in a meeting. The calm ones write them
formulas.first_frame: Two behaviours shown or named, the common one first.
formulas.trap: Name a behaviour the audience will recognise as what most people really do, or it reads as a straw man.

formulas.name: Old way, new way
formulas.spoken: We used to {old way}. Now everyone {new way}. Which is better for {goal}?
formulas.example: We kept launch notes in documents. Now it is one shared board. Which is better?
formulas.first_frame: A visual of the old way beside the new way, such as a document next to a board.
formulas.trap: The hook only works if the body answers and takes a side from real expertise.

formulas.name: The replacement
formulas.spoken: {This thing} replaced {expensive thing} for {price}
formulas.example: This one tool replaced the three we were paying for, at a third of the cost
formulas.first_frame: The old tools side by side, then one window taking their place
formulas.trap: Overstating the replacement. If it replaced part of the job, say which part, or the comments will say it for you.

formulas.name: Two real options
formulas.spoken: {Option A} or {Option B} for {specific decision}?
formulas.example: Kanban or a simple checklist for a team of five?
formulas.first_frame: Both options named on screen, split down the middle.
formulas.trap: Both options must be ones the audience really weighs, and the payoff must pick a side.

formulas.name: Versus, same job
formulas.spoken: {Option A} vs {Option B}: I {did the same job} in both.
formulas.example: Spreadsheet vs shared board: I planned the same launch in both.
formulas.first_frame: Both tools split on screen with the same task in each.
formulas.trap: A rigged comparison reads as sponsored; show the real trade-off.

formulas.name: Advice rejected
formulas.spoken: Everyone says {accepted advice}. I {did the opposite} and {result}
formulas.example: Everyone says add more integrations. I removed half of ours and support tickets dropped
formulas.on_screen: Everyone says this. I did not
formulas.first_frame: The common advice on screen, then crossed out by the real result
formulas.trap: Needs evidence in the next fifteen seconds or it reads as contrarian for its own sake.

formulas.name: Consensus backfires
formulas.spoken: Everyone says {X}. Here's why {X} is exactly why {bad outcome}.
formulas.example: Everyone says automate everything first. Here's why that's exactly why your workflows break.
formulas.first_frame: The popular advice on screen as a quote card or checklist item.
formulas.trap: Only works when the payoff really connects the advice to the bad outcome.

formulas.name: Does not work
formulas.spoken: {Popular thing} does not work the way people think. Here is why
formulas.example: Long onboarding tours do not work the way people think. Here is why
formulas.on_screen: Does not work how you think
formulas.first_frame: The popular thing running on screen, with the flaw circled
formulas.trap: Saying it does not work and then showing it does, a bit. Be exact about where it fails.

formulas.name: Drop the assumed need
formulas.spoken: You can {drop the thing the buyer believes they need}.
formulas.example: You can cancel your third scheduling tool.
formulas.first_frame: The thing being dropped on screen, such as a subscription list.
formulas.trap: Draws strong reactions including angry ones; stay fair to any named product and get legal review before naming a competitor in paid ads.

formulas.name: Everyone is missing
formulas.spoken: Everyone is doing {trend}, but they are missing {key detail}
formulas.example: Everyone is adding an AI chat box and missing the undo button
formulas.first_frame: The trend as a familiar screen, with the missing piece circled
formulas.trap: Naming a detail that is not actually missing. Check three real examples first.

formulas.name: Everyone thinks, wrongly
formulas.spoken: Everyone thinks {X} because {Y}. They're wrong, and here's what's actually happening.
formulas.example: Everyone thinks onboarding emails get ignored because they're too long. They're wrong, and here's what's actually happening.
formulas.on_screen: The real reason onboarding emails fail
formulas.first_frame: The common belief shown as text or a screenshot, about to be crossed out.
formulas.trap: Highest peak and highest variance; the body has to defend the claim or trust collapses.

formulas.name: The hidden cost
formulas.spoken: The hidden cost of {popular thing}
formulas.example: The hidden cost of free tools that do not talk to each other
formulas.on_screen: The hidden cost of free tools
formulas.first_frame: The popular thing on screen with a running tally beside it
formulas.trap: A cost with no working shown. Show the sum or it is only a feeling.

formulas.name: I stopped
formulas.spoken: I stopped {thing everyone does} and {result}
formulas.example: I stopped sending a weekly newsletter and replies to our team went up
formulas.first_frame: The thing being switched off or deleted on screen
formulas.trap: Claiming a result you cannot show. Put the before and after on screen.

formulas.name: Myth and reality
formulas.spoken: Myth: {popular belief}. Reality: {the truer version}
formulas.example: Myth: customers want every feature. Reality: they use three
formulas.first_frame: Two halves of the screen, the myth struck through, the reality beside it
formulas.trap: A myth nobody believed. Pick one you have actually heard people say.

formulas.name: Stop and swap
formulas.spoken: Stop {common action}. Do {alternative} instead
formulas.example: Stop sending a welcome email with six links. Send one link and a short video
formulas.first_frame: The habit being done on screen, then a red cross over it
formulas.trap: Telling people to stop doing something nobody does. The habit has to be one the viewer recognises in themselves.

formulas.name: Not this, but that
formulas.spoken: It is not {common cause}. It is {real cause}
formulas.example: It is not your server that is slow. It is one database query
formulas.first_frame: The usual suspect on screen, then crossed out for the real cause
formulas.trap: Swapping one vague cause for another. The real cause has to be shown.

formulas.name: The opposite is true
formulas.spoken: Why {common belief} is actually the opposite
formulas.example: Why giving trial users more features is the opposite of what helps them sign up
formulas.first_frame: The common belief on screen, then flipped
formulas.trap: Flipping a belief nobody holds. State the real thing within ten seconds.

formulas.name: Permission to skip it
formulas.spoken: You do not need {the thing everyone says you need}
formulas.example: You do not need a developer to add a booking form. You need ten minutes
formulas.on_screen: You do not need a developer
formulas.first_frame: The supposed requirement crossed out on screen
formulas.trap: Removing the blocker and putting nothing in its place. The second half is the whole video.

formulas.name: The practice is the cause
formulas.spoken: {Common practice} is exactly why you can't {goal}.
formulas.example: Weekly status meetings are exactly why you can't ship on Fridays.
formulas.first_frame: The common practice on screen, such as a calendar block.
formulas.trap: The causal link has to hold up in the body, or it reads as provocation.

formulas.name: Saying flipped
formulas.spoken: {Well-known saying, inverted}
formulas.example: The customer is not always right. The customer is always telling you something
formulas.first_frame: The familiar saying on screen with one word swapped
formulas.trap: Flipping a saying nobody says. The original has to be a reflex, or the inversion is just a sentence.

formulas.name: Stopped working
formulas.spoken: {Popular strategy} has stopped working for us. Here is what we do now
formulas.example: Cold calling has stopped working for us. Here is what we do now
formulas.first_frame: The old method shown, then replaced by the new one
formulas.trap: Declaring something dead on a hunch. Say what you measured and over how long.

formulas.name: Unpopular opinion
formulas.spoken: Unpopular opinion: {bold claim about your field}
formulas.example: Unpopular opinion: most onboarding tours should be deleted
formulas.first_frame: The claim on screen in plain type, nothing else
formulas.trap: An opinion nobody would argue with. If no one disagrees, it was only a statement.

formulas.name: After the milestone
formulas.spoken: What happens after {milestone} is the hard part
formulas.example: What happens after you launch the help centre is the hard part
formulas.first_frame: The milestone achieved on screen, the next step left empty.
formulas.trap: "Nobody talks about" with no named thing is on the source's own banned list; name the thing straight after.

formulas.name: Credibility, then gap
formulas.spoken: I've spent {time} doing {thing}. Here is what I would tell you first
formulas.example: I've spent six years answering support emails. Here is what I would tell you first
formulas.first_frame: The speaker or their real workspace, already mid-task.
formulas.trap: False authority reads worse than none; if you can't back the claim, leave it out.

formulas.name: Found something hidden
formulas.spoken: I found {hidden thing} in {familiar place} that {does unexpected thing}.
formulas.example: I found a setting in our billing page that stops failed-payment emails going to the wrong person.
formulas.first_frame: The familiar screen with the hidden thing highlighted.
formulas.trap: Hold back the answer but name the category of it, or the gap reads as bait.

formulas.name: Found out why
formulas.spoken: I found out why {common problem} keeps happening
formulas.example: I found out why our onboarding emails keep landing in spam
formulas.first_frame: The problem itself on screen, mid-failure, before anyone speaks
formulas.trap: Never answering the why. If the cause turns up after the halfway mark, the title has lied.

formulas.name: Quiet loss
formulas.spoken: Most {audience} lose {resource} to {thing} without noticing the one {detail} causing it.
formulas.example: Most small teams lose hours to meetings without noticing the one recurring invite causing it.
formulas.on_screen: The one invite costing you hours
formulas.first_frame: The recurring thing, such as a calendar full of the same invite.
formulas.trap: Specific enough to feel real, or the viewer files it as generic.

formulas.name: Number first
formulas.spoken: {Specific number}: that is how many {things} {context}
formulas.example: Forty-one: that is how many tabs I had open before we built this
formulas.first_frame: The number alone in large type, then the reason it matters
formulas.trap: A number with no payoff. Say why it matters in the next sentence.

formulas.name: Reason, but not that
formulas.spoken: There's a reason {surprising observation}, and it's not {expected explanation}.
formulas.example: There's a reason your reports look different on every machine, and it's not the software.
formulas.first_frame: The surprising observation itself shown, such as two mismatched screens.
formulas.trap: If the real reason is weak, the gap closes with a shrug.

formulas.name: One-line payoff
formulas.spoken: This one {setting or habit} {changed a result} and it's {off by default}.
formulas.example: This one setting made our reports easier to share and it's off by default.
formulas.on_screen: Off by default, worth switching on
formulas.first_frame: The setting on screen with the line written over it, already readable.
formulas.trap: No greeting, no logo, no slow zoom; the first frame is the whole funnel.

formulas.name: What happens when
formulas.spoken: What happens when you {unexpected action} for {timeframe}
formulas.example: What happens when you switch off every notification in your app for a week
formulas.first_frame: A timer or dashboard already running, day one marked on screen
formulas.trap: A setup with no stake. If nothing is at risk, the answer is a shrug.

formulas.name: Withheld reveal
formulas.spoken: I won't say which {thing}, but my {result} is {surprising}.
formulas.example: I won't say which export setting, but my reports now load before I've finished my coffee.
formulas.first_frame: The result on screen with the key detail blurred or covered.
formulas.trap: A reveal that never comes, or comes late, burns trust faster than no hook.

formulas.name: Withhold the noun
formulas.spoken: The {withheld noun} behind most {common frustration}.
formulas.example: The setting behind most missed meeting reminders.
formulas.first_frame: The frustration on screen, such as a notification that never arrived.
formulas.trap: Must pay off inside the video; a gap with no answer is clickbait and hurts what follows.

formulas.name: Before and after
formulas.spoken: {Show the old thing}. {Show the new thing}. {One sentence on the lever}
formulas.example: This was our checkout last March. This is it now. We removed one field
formulas.first_frame: The old version, then a hard cut to the new one
formulas.trap: Three levers. Name one thing that changed or the transformation stops being believable.

formulas.name: Behind the scenes
formulas.spoken: Behind the scenes of {thing worth seeing}
formulas.example: Behind the scenes of how we ship an update every Friday
formulas.first_frame: The real working space or screen, already in use
formulas.trap: Showing a tidy set instead of the real thing. The mess is the point.

formulas.name: Builds itself
formulas.spoken: {The claim, built word by word, as the thing connects}.
formulas.example: Connect your calendar to your project board. Watch it fill itself in.
formulas.first_frame: A cable or line connecting two real things as the claim builds word by word on screen.
formulas.trap: From one account's experience; keep the claim to what the next shot can really show.

formulas.name: Cold open demo
formulas.spoken: {Start mid-action, already doing the thing}. Watch what this does
formulas.example: Already dragging a file into the app. Watch what this does
formulas.first_frame: The screen already mid-action, a hand or cursor moving
formulas.trap: A result that takes twelve seconds to arrive. If the payoff is slow, cut to it and show the wait afterwards.

formulas.name: Look at this
formulas.spoken: Look at this. That's actually {surprise}.
formulas.example: Look at this. That one button is actually the whole report.
formulas.first_frame: The surprising thing already on screen, with a hand or cursor pointing at it.
formulas.trap: The spoken line is only a pointer, so a flat visual leaves nothing to point at.

formulas.name: Cold open on the peak
formulas.spoken: {Peak moment shown first}. To get here I had to {obstacle}, so let me show you.
formulas.example: That is the whole team on one board. It started as four spreadsheets
formulas.first_frame: A few seconds of the most striking moment, before any setup.
formulas.trap: The teased moment must appear later and be worth the wait.

formulas.name: The receipt shot
formulas.spoken: {Plain statement of the number or result on screen}.
formulas.example: Here's the real invoice total, and here's what we changed.
formulas.first_frame: A real number visible in frame one: an analytics screen, an invoice, a settings page.
formulas.trap: A fake or staged number gets caught and costs trust.

formulas.name: Result first, then rewind
formulas.spoken: {Finished result, shown}. Now let me back up to how it started.
formulas.example: This is the finished dashboard. Now let me back up to the blank page it started as.
formulas.first_frame: The finished result filling the frame before any setup appears.
formulas.trap: The result has to appear and be worth the wait, or it reads as a bait tease.

formulas.name: The video proves it
formulas.spoken: Nobody {did the usual thing} for this video. {The tool did}.
formulas.example: Nobody edited this video by hand. The tool did.
formulas.first_frame: The finished video itself, with the claim shown on screen as it plays.
formulas.trap: Only works if the claim is true and checkable; an unverifiable "nobody did this" damages trust.

formulas.name: Split before and after
formulas.spoken: {Before state}. {After state}. Here's what changed.
formulas.example: Empty dashboard on the left. A full one on the right. Here's what changed.
formulas.first_frame: Both states visible instantly, divided down the middle of the frame.
formulas.trap: Show a genuine result, not staged contrast.

formulas.name: The origin
formulas.spoken: Every {thing} we make starts in the same {place}. Here it is
formulas.example: Every video we make starts in the same short brief. Here it is
formulas.first_frame: The real file or template open full-frame
formulas.trap: Works once per channel. It is a reveal about you, and you only have one.

formulas.name: The reveal
formulas.spoken: This is the new {thing}
formulas.example: This is the new dashboard, and it finally lets you filter by team
formulas.first_frame: The product held up or filling the screen, already in motion
formulas.trap: Holding the thing up without saying what it changes. A reveal with no stake is an advert.

formulas.name: Two tools, joined
formulas.spoken: {Tool A} and {Tool B}, working together on {outcome}.
formulas.example: Your helpdesk and your chat tool, working together so nobody asks the same question twice.
formulas.first_frame: Two tools the viewer already knows side by side, joined by a line, a plus sign or a cable.
formulas.trap: From one account's own experience, not evidence; the tools must be ones your audience actually uses.

formulas.name: Typed live in the app
formulas.spoken: {The claim, typed live}. Now watch what it does.
formulas.example: Show me every task due this week. Now watch what it does.
formulas.first_frame: The claim being typed into the real product, then a cut to the product doing it.
formulas.trap: One account found the same line flopped as a static card and did better typed live, but that is a single account's experience.

formulas.name: Your first time
formulas.spoken: Never {done the task} before? Do this first
formulas.example: Never built a report before? Do this first
formulas.first_frame: The empty screen a beginner would see
formulas.trap: Assuming knowledge a first-timer does not have in the very next sentence.

formulas.name: In so many steps
formulas.spoken: {Result} in {N} steps. Step one: {first step}
formulas.example: A client portal in three steps. Step one: pick the pages they can see
formulas.on_screen: A client portal in three steps
formulas.first_frame: Step one already on screen, with the count beside it
formulas.trap: More steps than promised, or a first step that is really a prerequisite.

formulas.name: Start to finish
formulas.spoken: Here is how I {task}, start to finish
formulas.example: Here is how I set up a new client, start to finish
formulas.on_screen: A new client, start to finish
formulas.first_frame: The finished result for one second, then the blank start
formulas.trap: Skipping the dull middle step that is the one people get stuck on.

formulas.name: How to, without the pain
formulas.spoken: How to {desired result} without {pain point}.
formulas.example: How to send a client report without rebuilding it every month.
formulas.first_frame: The finished result on screen, with the pain point visible and fading.
formulas.trap: If the without-clause isn't actually delivered, the pre-screen turns into a broken promise.

formulas.name: The clock
formulas.spoken: In the next {time} you will have {specific result}
formulas.example: In the next six minutes you will have a working invoice template ready to send
formulas.on_screen: A working template in six minutes
formulas.first_frame: A visible timer starting at zero beside the empty starting screen
formulas.trap: The clock has to be true. Overrun it and the next video's hook is not believed.

formulas.name: The stack
formulas.spoken: {Tool A} plus {tool B} gives you {outcome} in {one step}
formulas.example: A form builder plus a spreadsheet gives you a weekly sign-up report in one step
formulas.first_frame: Both tool logos side by side, then the combined result
formulas.trap: Both tools must be nameable and the outcome must need both.

formulas.name: Result by odd method
formulas.spoken: {Person or team} got {result} using {unexpected method}.
formulas.example: One of our customers stopped chasing late invoices by using a plain spreadsheet export.
formulas.first_frame: The unexpected method itself on screen, such as the plain export.
formulas.trap: The method has to be real and specific; a named result with no named method sounds like a lecture.

formulas.name: Count with a tease
formulas.spoken: {N} {things} that {specific payoff}, and number {X} {surprised me}.
formulas.example: Seven small edits that made our demo clearer, and number four took two minutes.
formulas.on_screen: Seven edits, number four surprised me
formulas.first_frame: The first item, or the count, large on screen.
formulas.trap: The pure list is niche-dependent; the source's own sample found numbers worked better attached to a time or effort claim.

formulas.name: Numbered, with a favourite
formulas.spoken: {N} {things} that {outcome}. Number {k} is the one nobody uses
formulas.example: Five settings that make reports load faster. Number four is the one nobody touches
formulas.first_frame: A big number one on screen, with the list counting up
formulas.trap: N above seven. Nobody believes you have nine good ones, and you do not.

formulas.name: Only n things
formulas.spoken: The only {N} {things} you need to {result}
formulas.example: The only three settings you need to change in week one
formulas.first_frame: Three items lined up on screen, ready to count off
formulas.trap: A short list that quietly leaves out the one thing people really need.

formulas.name: The counted list
formulas.spoken: {N} things I would do differently if I {started again}
formulas.example: Seven things I would do differently if I rebuilt our onboarding from scratch
formulas.first_frame: The number large on screen with the first item already visible
formulas.trap: The count must be exact and every item must be different in kind.

formulas.name: Tools every role needs
formulas.spoken: {N} tools every {role} needs
formulas.example: Four tools every support lead should have open
formulas.first_frame: The tools' windows tiled on screen
formulas.trap: A list that is all affiliate links. Pick tools you use every day.

formulas.name: Underrated picks
formulas.spoken: {N} underrated {tools or habits} that save me {time}
formulas.example: Four underrated features in our own app that save me time every week
formulas.first_frame: The first feature in use, with a count in the corner
formulas.trap: Listing things that are not underrated at all. Pick ones people genuinely miss.

formulas.name: Wish I had known
formulas.spoken: {N} things I wish I had known at {stage}
formulas.example: Five things I wish I had known before our first hundred customers
formulas.on_screen: Things I wish I had known
formulas.first_frame: The stage or moment named on screen, with the first item ready
formulas.trap: Advice that is really a brag. Each item has to be a mistake or a lesson.

formulas.name: Wish I knew before
formulas.spoken: {N} {things} I wish I knew before I {did Y}.
formulas.example: Four things I wish I knew before I set up our first automation.
formulas.first_frame: The first item already numbered and on screen.
formulas.trap: Padding to hit a number dilutes the payoff; a short honest list beats a long weak one.

formulas.name: One thing capping you
formulas.spoken: You're doing everything right with {goal}, and one {hidden thing} is quietly capping your results.
formulas.example: You're doing everything right with onboarding, and one early email is quietly capping your activation.
formulas.first_frame: The area the viewer cares about on screen, with the hidden thing circled.
formulas.trap: Name what the hidden thing is within the video, or the setup is a tease with no end.

formulas.name: Mistakes to skip
formulas.spoken: {N} mistakes I made {doing thing}, so you can skip them
formulas.example: Five mistakes I made migrating our data, so you can skip them
formulas.first_frame: The first mistake already shown on screen as a real error
formulas.trap: Mistakes that are really humble brags. Name ones that cost something.

formulas.name: Stop doing this
formulas.spoken: Stop {common action}. You're {losing or wasting} {specific thing}.
formulas.example: Stop exporting reports as images. You're losing the data inside them.
formulas.first_frame: The common action in progress, with the cost visible.
formulas.trap: The source's own sample gave this no support for business content; the fix must arrive fast or it reads as fear-bait.

formulas.name: The mistake
formulas.spoken: {Your specific habit} is why {the bad result}. It is not {the usual suspect}
formulas.example: Your first thirty seconds are why people leave the trial. It is not the pricing
formulas.first_frame: The viewer's likely mistake shown on screen, ready to check in one second
formulas.trap: Only works if the mistake is common and the viewer can check it in one second.

formulas.name: The warning
formulas.spoken: Do not {next action} until you check {one thing}
formulas.example: Do not publish another page until you check this one setting
formulas.first_frame: The one setting or screen, highlighted before anything else
formulas.trap: If the cost is small the hook is a lie. Reserve it.

formulas.name: Wrong all along
formulas.spoken: I have been {doing thing} wrong for {long time}
formulas.example: I have been exporting reports by hand for two years
formulas.first_frame: The clumsy old way shown in full, mid-task
formulas.trap: Confessing to a mistake nobody makes. The viewer has to recognise the habit as theirs.

formulas.name: Wrong all along
formulas.spoken: You've been {doing everyday thing} wrong this whole time.
formulas.example: You've been naming your files wrong this whole time.
formulas.first_frame: The everyday action being done the usual way.
formulas.trap: A manufactured problem gets the view and loses the viewer; the correction must be real.

formulas.name: Wrong way, right way
formulas.spoken: You are doing {thing} wrong, and it is not your fault. {The fix}
formulas.example: Your invoice template is set up wrong, and it is not your fault
formulas.on_screen: Not your fault, here is the fix
formulas.first_frame: The wrong version on screen, with the problem circled
formulas.trap: Skipping the absolution. 'You are doing it wrong' on its own makes people leave rather than learn.

formulas.name: Cheat sheet
formulas.spoken: {Thing} cheat sheet, keep this one
formulas.example: Keyboard shortcuts cheat sheet, keep this one
formulas.first_frame: The finished sheet full-frame and readable at once
formulas.trap: A sheet too dense to read on a phone. Test it at phone size.

formulas.name: The first step is free
formulas.spoken: Start {doing the outcome} today, free for {period}
formulas.example: Start sending invoices today, free for thirty days
formulas.first_frame: The first step already done on screen: a sent invoice, a made board
formulas.trap: A free start that needs a card, a call or a form the film did not mention.

formulas.name: Now you can
formulas.spoken: You can now {do the new thing} in {product}
formulas.example: You can now assign a card from your inbox
formulas.first_frame: The new thing happening, cursor already on it
formulas.trap: Announcing the feature by its name instead of showing what it lets someone do.

formulas.name: The deal, said plainly
formulas.spoken: {Product} is {the deal} until {date}
formulas.example: The team plan is half price until Friday
formulas.first_frame: The deal in large type over the product in use
formulas.trap: A deadline that is not real, or a deal the viewer has to hunt for after the film.

formulas.name: Nothing to lose
formulas.spoken: Try {product} on {your real task}. If it does not {outcome}, you have lost {a small thing}
formulas.example: Try it on this week's rota. If it is not quicker, you have lost ten minutes
formulas.first_frame: The real task open, half done
formulas.trap: Promising an outcome the product cannot show inside the trial.

formulas.name: What you get for it
formulas.spoken: For {price}, you get {three concrete things}
formulas.example: For nine pounds a month you get the boards, the reminders and the shared inbox
formulas.first_frame: The three things on screen at once, each one real product
formulas.trap: Listing features instead of things the viewer will use this week.

formulas.name: Problem, then offer
formulas.spoken: {Problem line}. We built {thing} for it, and you can {low-risk first step} today.
formulas.example: Tracking leave on a sheet gets messy. Try our leave calendar free today
formulas.first_frame: The messy current state on screen, with the product's cleaner version about to replace it.
formulas.trap: On cold audiences an offer in the first seconds reads as a pitch, so soften it up front.

formulas.name: The deadline
formulas.spoken: {Thing} changes on {date}. Do {action} before then
formulas.example: The old import format stops working on the first of March. Re-export your files before then
formulas.first_frame: The date shown on a calendar or banner, with the thing it affects beside it
formulas.trap: Manufactured urgency. One fake deadline and every future one is discounted.

formulas.name: Steal this
formulas.spoken: Steal this {artifact}. It took me {time} to get right
formulas.example: Steal this onboarding checklist. It took me a month to get right
formulas.first_frame: The finished artifact full-frame and readable, with a cursor ready to copy it
formulas.trap: The artifact not being on screen. If they cannot screenshot it, there is nothing to steal.

formulas.name: Near-future claim
formulas.spoken: This {thing} is about to change how {audience} {action}.
formulas.example: This one view is about to change how support teams sort their inbox.
formulas.first_frame: The new view already open and being used, mid-task.
formulas.trap: A prediction with no demo behind it reads as noise, so show the change happening.

formulas.name: Only one that
formulas.spoken: This is the only {product type} that {outcome}.
formulas.example: This is the only invoice tool that chases the client for you without a template to maintain.
formulas.first_frame: The outcome happening in the product, not the logo.
formulas.trap: Only for claims you can defend; an indefensible "only" is also a compliance risk.

formulas.name: Restate and raise
formulas.spoken: {The title's promise in spoken voice}. {The obstacle or stakes}. By the end you'll {capability}.
formulas.example: Automated reminders, set up today. Most teams get one rule wrong
formulas.first_frame: The thing being built, open and ready, with no intro card.
formulas.trap: Don't summarise the whole video in the hook; confirm the promise and open the loop.

formulas.name: Result, not the cause
formulas.spoken: {Impressive result}, and it had nothing to do with {expected cause}.
formulas.example: One page brought far more demo requests, and it was not the copy
formulas.on_screen: More demo requests, not the copy
formulas.first_frame: The result on screen, with the expected cause conspicuously absent.
formulas.trap: Skip it when you can't show or explain the real cause, since that is what the viewer stays for.

formulas.name: Specific bold claim
formulas.spoken: This replaced my entire {routine}.
formulas.example: This replaced my whole Monday reporting routine.
formulas.first_frame: The routine's old artefacts next to the replacement already running.
formulas.trap: A bold claim needs substantiation on screen or in the next beat.

formulas.name: The superlative
formulas.spoken: The {fastest, biggest or only} {thing} is {the answer}
formulas.example: The fastest way to get a new teammate set up is a recorded walkthrough they can pause
formulas.first_frame: The answer itself on screen, not a title card
formulas.trap: A superlative with a soft answer. If the second half is 'consistency', you have said nothing and the comments will tell you.

formulas.name: Time collapse
formulas.spoken: This used to take me {long time}. It now takes {short time}
formulas.example: Writing a proposal used to take me an afternoon. Now it takes twenty minutes
formulas.first_frame: A clock or timer in the corner, running as the task gets done
formulas.trap: A ratio nobody believes. A huge drop gets treated as a lie even when it is true.

formulas.name: Counter climbs
formulas.spoken: {Short claim as a number moves}.
formulas.example: Watch this number as I switch it on.
formulas.first_frame: A counter already moving from frame one, locking on a figure at the end of the hook.
formulas.trap: The number must be real and must lock on something; a counter that goes nowhere is a gimmick.

formulas.name: Caught mid-action
formulas.spoken: {Short line that names what just happened}.
formulas.example: Whoops. That's three hours of work, gone.
formulas.first_frame: Someone caught mid-motion, such as wincing at a screen or tearing up a page.
formulas.trap: The motion has to be real and relevant; a random jolt with no link to the topic is just noise.

formulas.name: Mid-sentence start
formulas.spoken: ...and that is when {the turn}
formulas.example: ...and that is when the customer asked for a refund. Three days after approving the design
formulas.first_frame: A cut that lands mid-scene, with no title card or greeting
formulas.trap: Never going back to fill in the gap. Deliver the setup by second eight or it reads as a mistake.

formulas.name: The odd object
formulas.spoken: This {out-of-place object} is the reason {outcome}.
formulas.example: This two-pound kitchen timer is the reason our team stopped overrunning meetings.
formulas.first_frame: An out-of-place item held to camera, with nothing else competing.
formulas.trap: The mismatch is the gap, so the object must connect to the payoff.

formulas.name: Countdown challenge
formulas.spoken: {Timer or challenge shown}: by the end you'll have {payoff}.
formulas.example: Sixty seconds on the clock: by the end you'll have a working form.
formulas.first_frame: A timer already running over the starting screen.
formulas.trap: If the payoff doesn't arrive before the timer ends, hold rate falls away.

formulas.name: Point of view
formulas.spoken: POV: you are {scenario}
formulas.example: POV: you are a support agent and the same ticket arrives for the ninth time today
formulas.first_frame: A first-person view of the scene, already under way
formulas.trap: A scenario that fits no one. Make it specific enough to be recognised.

formulas.name: Their view of the problem
formulas.spoken: {Short line the viewer would say about this view}.
formulas.example: Forty-seven tabs. Again.
formulas.first_frame: The viewer's own view of the pain: a crowded browser, an inbox, an alarm.
formulas.trap: Needs a view the audience really recognises, not a generic mess.

formulas.name: Something breaks
formulas.spoken: {Short line describing what just broke}.
formulas.example: That's the old way of tracking leave, gone.
formulas.first_frame: A recognisable object on screen that visibly breaks, burns or collapses in the first beat.
formulas.trap: The break has to mean something about the topic; spectacle alone doesn't carry it.

formulas.name: The hard-to-believe claim
formulas.spoken: You can {outcome that sounds untrue} without {the usual cost}
formulas.example: You can move a whole help centre across without copying a single page by hand
formulas.first_frame: The result starting to happen on screen within the first second
formulas.trap: The proof has to start within twenty seconds or it reads as clickbait.

formulas.name: The ratio
formulas.spoken: {Number} to {number}: the ratio that matters
formulas.example: Three to one: our ratio of bug fixes to new features last quarter
formulas.first_frame: The two numbers in large type, one above the other
formulas.trap: A ratio you invented for effect. Use one you track.

formulas.name: Name the pain, sharpen it
formulas.spoken: {Pain named}. It gets worse when {agitation}. {Fix} sorts it out.
formulas.example: Your invoices go out late, and then the client asks. One reminder rule fixes it
formulas.on_screen: Late invoices, fixed with one rule
formulas.first_frame: The pain moment on screen, such as the unanswered client email.
formulas.trap: Spending the whole hook on agitation leaves nothing for the fix; keep the fix in view.

formulas.name: The trap
formulas.spoken: The harder you try to {goal}, the worse {outcome} gets. Here's the trap.
formulas.example: The harder you try to keep every task updated, the worse your board gets. Here's the trap.
formulas.first_frame: The effortful state on screen, such as a crowded board.
formulas.trap: Needs a genuine mechanism; "here's the trap" without one is empty.

formulas.name: You are not the problem
formulas.spoken: You are not {negative self-belief}. You just need {solution}
formulas.example: You are not bad at spreadsheets. You just need the template filled in for you
formulas.first_frame: The blank or messy starting point, then the solution filling it in
formulas.trap: Flattery with no fix. The solution has to be shown, not just named.

formulas.name: Not you, the setup
formulas.spoken: You're not {self-blame}. You're {reframe}.
formulas.example: You're not disorganised. You're using a tool built for a different team size.
formulas.first_frame: The viewer's own messy-but-real workspace in frame.
formulas.trap: A reframe that doesn't fit their situation reads as flattery.

formulas.name: Point of view moment
formulas.spoken: POV: it's {specific moment} and you're {specific action}.
formulas.example: POV: it's the end of the month and you're still matching receipts by hand.
formulas.first_frame: The viewer's-eye view of the moment, with the screen or object in shot.
formulas.trap: Specificity is the whole mechanic; a generic POV is invisible.

formulas.name: Stop blaming
formulas.spoken: Stop blaming {usual suspect}. The real issue is {cause}
formulas.example: Stop blaming the free plan. The real issue is the first screen
formulas.first_frame: The usual suspect on screen, then the real cause lit up
formulas.trap: Blaming the viewer instead. The tone must be on their side.

formulas.name: That feeling
formulas.spoken: That feeling when {hyper-specific shared moment}? There's a fix.
formulas.example: That feeling when a client says quick question at six on a Friday? There's a fix.
formulas.first_frame: The exact moment as a message or notification on screen.
formulas.trap: The moment must be one your audience really recognises; otherwise nobody feels it.

formulas.name: The objection
formulas.spoken: "{Objection they actually say}". Fine. Here is the version that works anyway
formulas.example: "I hate being on camera." Fine. Here is the version where your face never appears
formulas.first_frame: The objection as a real comment or message on screen
formulas.trap: Inventing the objection. Pull it verbatim from a message or comment, including the bad grammar.

formulas.name: Three short lines
formulas.spoken: The {relatable enemy} is {negative thing}. The {hero} is {strong positive}. And I {accelerant}. {Teaser question}?
formulas.example: The status meeting is dead time. The shared board is the fix. Want to see it?
formulas.first_frame: Three lines appearing one at a time on a plain background, then cutting to the board.
formulas.trap: Built for feed text; spoken at full pace it can run past the deadline, so time it aloud.

formulas.name: What it costs
formulas.spoken: {Amount}: what {common thing} really costs
formulas.example: Two hundred pounds a month: what our unused seats really cost
formulas.first_frame: The sum worked out on screen, line by line
formulas.trap: A cost with no working shown. Show the sum or it is only a feeling.

formulas.name: All do this
formulas.spoken: All {N} of our {best customers} do this one thing
formulas.example: All twelve of our longest-standing customers set up this one rule on day one
formulas.first_frame: The one thing on screen, with the customers' names or logos around it
formulas.trap: Cherry-picking a group that fits. Say how you chose them.

formulas.name: Helped many
formulas.spoken: I have helped {N} {people} do {result}. The mistake I see most is {mistake}
formulas.example: I have helped forty teams set up billing. The mistake I see most is skipping test mode
formulas.first_frame: The common mistake on screen, with the count of teams helped beside it
formulas.trap: Inflating the number. Use the real count, even if it is small.

formulas.name: Inside view
formulas.spoken: I spent {N years} {inside the thing}. Here is what I saw from the inside
formulas.example: I spent six years on a support desk. Here is what I saw from the inside
formulas.on_screen: Six years on a support desk
formulas.first_frame: The speaker in the real workplace or setting, with the years on screen
formulas.trap: Promising an inside story and delivering the brochure. The comments are merciless about this one.

formulas.name: Metric moved
formulas.spoken: Our {metric} went from {before} to {after} when we changed {one thing}
formulas.example: Our trial sign-ups went from nine a day to fourteen when we changed the button label
formulas.first_frame: The before and after figures in large type, with the one change beneath
formulas.trap: Changing several things and crediting one. Name only what you actually changed.

formulas.name: Odd number lead
formulas.spoken: {Specific number} {units} of {thing}, and here's the one pattern that held.
formulas.example: Four hundred and twelve support tickets read by hand, and here's the one pattern that held.
formulas.first_frame: The raw material, such as a long list or folder, with the count visible.
formulas.trap: A made-up or rounded-up number gets spotted; use a real count you can show.

formulas.name: Receipt first
formulas.spoken: {Result or receipt shown}. Here's how it happened.
formulas.example: Here's the support queue at zero on a Friday afternoon. Here's how it happened.
formulas.first_frame: The result or receipt filling the frame, readable at a glance.
formulas.trap: Strongest when the proof stands on its own; a weak receipt makes the claim look thinner.

formulas.name: Result and breakdown
formulas.spoken: I {result} in {short timeframe}. Here is how it went
formulas.example: I rebuilt our help centre in a fortnight. Here is how it went
formulas.first_frame: The finished result full-frame and already moving
formulas.trap: A result with no evidence on screen. Show the thing, not the claim.

formulas.name: Someone else's result
formulas.spoken: There was one {person} who {outcome} in {time}
formulas.example: There was one customer who cut their support backlog in half within a quarter
formulas.first_frame: The named person or company, shown with their own screen
formulas.trap: No name and no link. An anonymous miracle is a rumour.

formulas.name: Spent so you needn't
formulas.spoken: I spent {time or money} on {thing} so you do not have to
formulas.example: I spent a month testing screen recorders so you do not have to
formulas.first_frame: The pile of things tried, shown on screen
formulas.trap: Spending nothing. The cost has to be real and shown.

formulas.name: Tested for a stretch
formulas.spoken: I {did X} for {time} to find out {Y}.
formulas.example: I ran every stand-up through the app for a month. Did it save time?
formulas.first_frame: A calendar or log of the test period filling up as the clip starts.
formulas.trap: Visible effort is the credibility, so a vague test with no real record behind it buys nothing.

formulas.name: Tested many
formulas.spoken: I tested {N} {options}. Only {one} did the job
formulas.example: I tested six form builders. Only one handled file uploads properly
formulas.first_frame: A grid of the options with a result mark on each
formulas.trap: A test with no criteria. Say what the job was before you show the winner.

formulas.name: The receipt
formulas.spoken: I {did thing} for {N days}. Here are the actual numbers
formulas.example: One product clip a day for sixty days. Here is what it did to sign-ups
formulas.first_frame: The real dashboard on screen, scrolled to the figures
formulas.trap: Not showing the screen. A numbers video with no screen recording is a numbers claim.

formulas.name: The number
formulas.spoken: {Number} of {group} {surprising fact}
formulas.example: Most people who download a new app never open it a second time
formulas.first_frame: The figure alone in large type with its source line beneath
formulas.trap: A statistic you cannot source. Say where it came from in the video or do not use it.

formulas.name: The teardown
formulas.spoken: I took {N} {real examples} apart and found {what they share}
formulas.example: I took nine competitor onboarding flows apart and found the one step they all skip
formulas.first_frame: A grid of the real examples on screen, with the shared part highlighted
formulas.trap: Name what you pulled and how many. A teardown of one example is an anecdote.

formulas.name: The buyer's own question
formulas.spoken: {The exact question the buyer would type into search}?
formulas.example: How do I stop getting double-booked on shared calendars?
formulas.first_frame: The question typed into a search box or chat field.
formulas.trap: Use the buyer's wording from reviews and comments, not marketing paraphrase.

formulas.name: Can you guess
formulas.spoken: Can you guess {surprising number or fact}?
formulas.example: Can you guess how many clicks it takes to cancel in most apps?
formulas.first_frame: The question in plain type over a blank field, ready to fill
formulas.trap: A number you cannot back up. Reveal it honestly within seconds.

formulas.name: Making this mistake
formulas.spoken: Are you making this {field} mistake?
formulas.example: Are you making this password-reset mistake in your app?
formulas.first_frame: The mistake on screen in a real screen the viewer would use
formulas.trap: A mistake the viewer cannot check. Let them test themselves in seconds.

formulas.name: Question, short answer, bonus
formulas.spoken: {The exact question, asked plainly}. Short answer: {real partial answer}. Stick around for {bonus}.
formulas.example: Can you merge two workspaces? Yes. What matters is what happens to your history
formulas.first_frame: The question on screen as the app is already open.
formulas.trap: A hollow short answer makes viewers leave the moment they notice.

formulas.name: State it, then doubt it
formulas.spoken: You need {widely accepted requirement}. Or do you?
formulas.example: You need a separate tool for every client. Or do you?
formulas.first_frame: The accepted idea as plain text, then a visible question mark.
formulas.trap: The source marks this as still being tested by practitioners; the doubt needs a real answer in the body.

formulas.name: The question as asked
formulas.spoken: "{Question exactly as it was asked}". I get this every week
formulas.example: "How do I get my data out of the old tool?" I get this every week
formulas.first_frame: The question in a message bubble, typos left in
formulas.trap: Tidying the question up. The value is that it is in their words, typos and all.

formulas.name: What would you do
formulas.spoken: What would you do if {scenario}?
formulas.example: What would you do if your biggest customer asked for their data tomorrow?
formulas.first_frame: The scenario acted out or shown on screen, still unresolved
formulas.trap: A scenario so remote it feels invented. Use one that has happened to someone real.

formulas.name: Why does it do that
formulas.spoken: Why does {common thing} {do the odd thing}?
formulas.example: Why does every signup form ask for your phone number?
formulas.first_frame: The familiar thing on screen, looking ordinary
formulas.trap: A question with a dull answer. Make sure the reason is worth waiting for.

formulas.name: Why does it keep happening
formulas.spoken: Why does {common annoyance} keep happening?
formulas.example: Why does your invoice keep showing the wrong currency?
formulas.first_frame: The annoyance happening on screen, in a real window
formulas.trap: Asking a question you do not answer. The viewer is owed the reason.

formulas.name: Almost gave up
formulas.spoken: I almost gave up on {thing} until {turning point}
formulas.example: I almost gave up on our onboarding flow until a customer filmed herself using it
formulas.first_frame: The low point on screen, such as an empty dashboard, before the turn
formulas.trap: A turning point that is vague. The viewer needs the exact thing that changed.

formulas.name: Cost confession
formulas.spoken: {Specific amount} is what {one mistake} cost me
formulas.example: Four hours a week is what one manual export cost our support team
formulas.on_screen: The mistake that cost real time
formulas.first_frame: The real number in large type over the screen where the mistake happened
formulas.trap: A fake cost. 'It cost me my peace of mind' is not a number and everybody can hear that.

formulas.name: The day I realised
formulas.spoken: The day I realised {insight}
formulas.example: The day I realised nobody had opened our settings page in a year
formulas.first_frame: The screen or data that triggered the realisation
formulas.trap: An insight that was obvious all along. Give the viewer the moment, not the moral.

formulas.name: Day it turned
formulas.spoken: I did {action} every day for {timeframe}. What happened on day {N} changed how I {activity}.
formulas.example: One customer email a day for ninety days. Day forty changed how I write
formulas.first_frame: A day counter on screen at the pivotal day.
formulas.trap: The day has to be a real turn, not decoration.

formulas.name: Doing it wrong
formulas.spoken: I was doing {common thing} completely wrong.
formulas.example: I was exporting my reports completely wrong.
formulas.first_frame: The old way mid-action, so the mistake is visible.
formulas.trap: Reads fake without lived-in detail about what exactly went wrong.

formulas.name: The flop record
formulas.spoken: My first {N} {attempts} did nothing. Here is what changed on {N plus one}
formulas.example: My first nine onboarding emails did nothing. Here is what changed on the tenth
formulas.first_frame: A list of the earlier attempts with their poor results, then the one that worked
formulas.trap: Making the change sound like luck. If the answer is 'I got lucky', there is no video.

formulas.name: Followed it, it failed
formulas.spoken: I followed {system or authority} perfectly. It failed. Then I broke one rule.
formulas.example: I followed the standard onboarding checklist perfectly. It failed. Then I broke one rule.
formulas.on_screen: The checklist failed, so I broke it
formulas.first_frame: The system or checklist on screen, followed to the letter.
formulas.trap: A story opener; lead with the failure, not the chronology.

formulas.name: I tried it
formulas.spoken: I {did the experiment} for {time}. {The stated cost}
formulas.example: A week in our own app with keyboard shortcuts only. The mouse went in a drawer
formulas.first_frame: The experiment set up in the real place, with the day count shown
formulas.trap: Needs a real cost (time, money or risk) or there is no stake.

formulas.name: I will admit it
formulas.spoken: I will admit it: I {confession}
formulas.example: I will admit it: I shipped that update without testing it on a phone
formulas.first_frame: The speaker or screen, straight on, with no polish
formulas.trap: A confession that is really a boast. It has to cost you something.

formulas.name: Last week
formulas.spoken: Last week, {unexpected thing} happened
formulas.example: Last week, a customer sent us a screen recording of their whole workday
formulas.first_frame: The unexpected thing shown straight away, such as the message itself
formulas.trap: An event that was not that unexpected. Start from the surprising detail.

formulas.name: Learned from
formulas.spoken: What I learned from {unusual source} about {topic}
formulas.example: What I learned from a bakery queue about onboarding
formulas.first_frame: The unusual source filmed in its own setting
formulas.trap: A strange source with no real link. The lesson has to follow from it, not be bolted on.

formulas.name: Real talk
formulas.spoken: Real talk: {honest admission}
formulas.example: Real talk: our first version only worked in one browser
formulas.first_frame: The old version on screen in its rough state
formulas.trap: An admission with no follow-up. Say what you did about it.

formulas.name: Someone else's story
formulas.spoken: How {named person or type of team} built {outcome} from {starting point}.
formulas.example: How a three-person support team built a help centre from a single shared document.
formulas.first_frame: The customer or team in their own setting, or the starting document.
formulas.trap: The story must be real and checkable, and a customer story needs the customer's agreement.

formulas.name: Cost confession
formulas.spoken: I spent {cost} so you don't have to. Here's what I learned.
formulas.example: I trialled seven scheduling tools over a quarter so you don't have to. Here's what I learned.
formulas.on_screen: Seven tools tested, so you don't
formulas.first_frame: A stack of the tools' tabs or logos being closed one by one.
formulas.trap: A vague "I did a lot of research" buys nothing; the receipt has to be real.

formulas.name: Then and now
formulas.spoken: {Time} ago I was {low point}. Today {high point}
formulas.example: Two years ago our whole product was a spreadsheet. Today it runs for four hundred teams
formulas.first_frame: The old state and the current state side by side
formulas.trap: A glow-up with nothing in the middle. Say what changed between the two.

formulas.name: Years, one lesson
formulas.spoken: {N years} of {experience} taught me one thing
formulas.example: Six years of building onboarding taught me one thing
formulas.first_frame: The speaker in their real working setting with the years on screen
formulas.trap: A lesson everyone already knows. If it fits on a poster, cut it.
